name: Developmental Editing
title: Developmental Editing
answer: Developmental editing is the structural work on a manuscript or narrative: shaping plot, character arcs, pacing, point of view, theme, and overall architecture before line editing or copyediting. In the context of AI, the scope includes using language models to analyze a draft's structure, identify inconsistencies, suggest alternative narrative paths, and generate editorial memos or reverse outlines. It also covers the design of interactive or branching narratives where AI may help map story logic and player or reader choices. The work is distinct from proofreading or style editing, focusing instead on whether the story works as a whole.

sections.body: Developmental editing is the structural work on a manuscript or narrative: shaping plot, character arcs, pacing, point of view, theme, and overall architecture before line editing or copyediting. In the context of AI, the scope includes using language models to analyze a draft's structure, identify inconsistencies, suggest alternative narrative paths, and generate editorial memos or reverse outlines. It also covers the design of interactive or branching narratives where AI may help map story logic and player or reader choices. The work is distinct from proofreading or style editing, focusing instead on whether the story works as a whole.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: AI-assisted developmental editing typically runs on large language models accessed through writing platforms, standalone chat interfaces, or local models run on a writer's own machine. These systems rely on cloud computing for the largest models, while smaller open-weight models can run on a standard laptop with sufficient memory. The infrastructure also includes document processing pipelines that convert manuscripts into chunks or embeddings so the model can reason over long texts without losing context. Many editors use a combination of general-purpose models and specialized writing tools that wrap those models in a manuscript-friendly interface.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a close reading of the manuscript, often supported by an AI-generated reverse outline that lists scenes, beats, or chapters in order. The editor then prompts the model to identify structural problems such as sagging middles, unresolved subplots, inconsistent character motivation, or shifts in tone. The model's output is treated as a draft of observations, which the editor verifies against the actual text and refines into an editorial letter or margin notes. In narrative design, the method may include using AI to simulate reader or player paths through a branching story and flag dead ends or weak branches.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on confidentiality, consent, and provenance. An editor should not upload a client's unpublished manuscript to a third-party AI service without explicit permission, because the text may be used for model training or retained in logs. Contracts and editorial agreements increasingly need to state whether AI tools are permitted, how outputs are attributed, and who owns any generated suggestions. There is also a risk that a model reproduces passages from its training data, so editors must check AI-generated text for unintended similarity to existing works. This is a matter of professional practice and contract drafting, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: AI-assisted developmental editing is moving toward more interactive and iterative workflows, where an editor and a model exchange drafts of structural analysis rather than one-off prompts. Models are likely to become better at holding a whole novel in context and at comparing multiple drafts of the same scene. The role of the human editor will shift toward judgment, taste, and author relationship, while the mechanical work of summarizing and cross-referencing is increasingly automated. The core question will remain whether the story works, and that answer still requires a human reader.
